paragraphs.text: When the angels formed the heavenly choir, they brought good news to the shepherds, saying: “We bring you good news today of great joy, which will be for all the people.” So we too borrow our words from those holy angels, and we bring you good news today: today the Church is at peace and the heretics are in turmoil. Today the ship of the Church rides in calm and comes to anchor in the stormless harbour of peace, while the madness of the heretics is tossed by its own breakers. Today the shepherds are free of care and the flock is safe; the enemies are at a loss, the wolves are helpless. Today the Saviour's vineyard flourishes and the workers of wickedness are dispirited. Today the people of God are exalted and the enemies of the truth are humbled. Today Christ rejoices and the devil mourns. Today the angels are glad and rejoice, and the demons run away in shame. Why say more? Today Christ, the King of peace, has come forth with his own peace and has banished all enmity, all grief and all pettiness. The sun shines upon the sky, but peace gives light to the Church of Christ. Peace is a longed-for name; peace is the bright profession of godliness; peace is the pure gaze of the priesthood; peace is the radiant beauty of the altar. What can we say that is worthy of peace, which is the very name of Christ? For Paul, speaking of Christ, says: “Christ is our peace, who has made both one.” The two were not divided in mind or cut apart in faith; they were separated by the envy of the devil. But just as, when an emperor makes a procession, the streets are swept and the colonnades are garlanded with every kind of ornament, so that nothing unworthy of the emperor's eyes may be seen, so as Christ the King of peace came forth, everything grievous withdrew out of our way. Truth has shone out, and falsehood runs away. Concord has shone out, and discord has fled. Often, when the best painters depict emperors, or brothers, or rulers and want to show the union of their souls, they set Concord behind them in the form of a woman, embracing those who are united with both her arms, to show that bodies which are separate are joined in mind. In the same way the peace of Christ has stepped in between those who stood apart and joined them together, and the prophet's word has been fulfilled in us: “And there shall be a counsel of peace between them both.”

On the previous day, then, our common father began with the greeting of the Gospel, the word of peace. Today it is we who take the lead in speaking of peace. Yesterday he greeted us with open hands through the word of truth, and today we, so to speak, receive him with wide-open arms and the gifts of peace. The war is over, and the beauty of peace shines out. Now the devil groans. Now the host of demons mourns. Now the flock exults. Now heaven rejoices. Today Peace dances, she who shares the life of the angels in heaven and shares the tent of the saints on earth. Peace is the hymn of the angels and the work of the saints. And see how wonderful it is: the things of heaven sing of peace, and the things of earth sing of peace. But when the angels in heaven sing of peace, they send it down to earth and make the rays of peace shine upon the earth; and when the saints on earth sing of it, they send its brilliance back up to heaven. The angels from heaven sing and say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace.” Do you see how the heavenly ranks send one another the gifts of peace? The angels in heaven announce peace to the earth. And when that devout choir sang to Christ, saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” this was added as well: “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest.” So let us too say: “Glory to God in the highest,” who has humbled the devil and exalted his own people. “Glory to God in the highest,” who has banished enmity and awarded us peace.

Let us tell you the devil's craft, though even before we speak you were not ignorant of his designs. Satan saw the Church walled about with faith. He saw her crowned with the doctrines of godliness. He saw, and seeing he wasted away; seeing he raged; seeing he went mad. He tried to scatter the glory of Christ, but he could not. For neither is the glory of Christ undone, nor is the peace of the priests destroyed. His wickedness gained him nothing, for the concord of the brothers took the lead in speaking of peace. For Christ is our peace. Let the peace of Christ rule in our hearts.

Pay careful attention to how God unfolds the beauty of peace and shows it flourishing in the prophets, shining in the apostles and dancing among the martyrs. Apart from peace nothing can stand, whether in heaven or on earth. Peace is the mouth of the Law. Peace is the tongue of the prophets. Peace is the teaching of the apostles. Peace is the desire of the martyrs and the prophets. What was the prophets' desire? “O Lord our God, give us peace.” The King received the petition. He had to sign it and give a fitting answer to the petition in his rescript. “What do you want,” he says, “you men brought up in godliness?” “O Lord our God, give us peace.” “I grant the favour; I sign it and write my reply.” The King signed it with his own hand: “I fulfil your petition.” When the prophets said, “O Lord our God, give us peace,” what then does he answer them through the grace of the Gospel? “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you.” Why “I give”? Why “I leave”? Because the whole [?] of Christ is seen both according to the flesh and according to the Godhead. He was departing according to the flesh while remaining according to the Godhead. So he said both “I leave” and “I give”: “I leave” as one being taken up, “I give” as one who still dwells among us. And peace was written in as the warrant for the apostles' journey. For just as warrants for the public post are invalid unless they are sealed by the emperor's hand, so the apostles' journey, had it not received the warrant of peace, could not have passed through a world full of war. What sort of warrant that peace is, let Isaiah tell: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things, of those who bring good news of peace, of those who bring good news of good things!” Do you see the warrant of peace? Hear also the opening of the Gospel message. The opening of the Gospel message is peace. Hear the Saviour saying: “Whatever city or house you enter, say, ‘Peace to this house.’” Peace steadies the priest's soul; it gives open ears to those who listen. For before any words, peace shines out and enlightens the minds of the hearers. It was because of this ancient character of the priesthood that God, extolling it, said: “He walked with you in peace, guiding aright, and turned many away from iniquity,” for “the lips of a priest guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord Almighty.” You see the reins and bridle of the priesthood: peace is the bridle of those who are guided. Do you want to learn something else, something unusual? Peace is the first and ancient name of the altar. For in the beginning an altar was called “peace,” since at the altar all pettiness, grief and enmity are dissolved. From the beginning God fixed the name “Peace” upon the altar. Where do we learn this? “And Gideon built an altar to the Lord and called its name ‘The Peace of the Lord.’”

Do you want to find the boundaries of godliness? Peace is the boundary, as of some wide and great country that is subject to different lords. The boundary walls show how far one man's lordship reaches and where another's holding begins. In the same way, since between the demons and Christ, who awards peace, lie the failings or the good deeds of human souls, some loving Christ and his peace and others running to the demons, the word of truth sets peace as the boundary, so that you may learn that as long as you see peace, there is the lordship of Christ. Whatever lies outside peace is foreign to Christ. Where do we learn this? Let David tell you; let the ancient surveyor of godliness point out the boundaries to you, he who says: “The lines have fallen to me in the best places, and indeed my inheritance is most excellent to me.” Pointing out the boundaries to us, he says: “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you; he makes peace your borders.”

Do you see the boundaries of peace, the everlasting boundaries that the prophets and apostles fixed? Learn something else as well. Joseph's brothers were once suspected of being spies. Having no other defence, they ran to the weapon of peace: “We are not spies; we are peaceable men.” Again, blessed David, raising the power of godliness on high and showing what the sinews and strength of truth are, says, addressing the ancient and holy city: “Let there be peace in your strength, and abundance among those who love you.” Again God, wishing to show that in war multitudes are destroyed and human prosperity is scattered, but in the word of peace they are gathered together, says through the prophet Ezekiel: “Let a plant of peace spring up for them, and they shall no longer be few.” For just as people arm themselves against wild beasts, and as soon as they appear armed they put the beasts to flight, so when peace appears war is scattered, devilish thoughts are scattered, and the phalanx of demons breaks up. For where there is peace, wickedness is put to flight, as wild beasts flee from a saint. That is why God says: “I will make a covenant of peace with David and will destroy the wild beasts.” Peace is a field of truth, a vineyard of righteousness and a river of godliness.

Do you see how peace has filled the spiritual Church like the streams of rivers? Do you see how the crowds flowing in from every side imitate the rushing streams of the river that make glad the city of God? And your rejoicing over this peace imitates the waves of the sea, which follow one upon another in their course, give way to one another and roll over one another without tumult. It does not rise up in rivalry but in harmony of disposition. Do you want to learn from the Scriptures, as well as from what you see, that peace is like a river? “Your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea.” But, as I said before, the divine trumpet that proclaims the word of peace has gone ahead of us. Let us too today follow the word of peace, and let us open the doors to it as if with both hands and say: “Open the gates; let a people enter that keeps righteousness and keeps peace, that lays hold of truth for ever.” Peace is a cargo [?], and the waves of the sea, and the shining sun. But why do I say the sun? The sun does not shine as brightly as the light that flashes from the Saviour's peace. For I see the sun subject to measure; its course comes to an end in the evening. But the peace of Christ, full of light, shines by day, gives light by night and flashes forth for ever. Listen. When peace appears, she does not appear alone; she will not come forward alone, but brings with her her sister, righteousness. Hear the prophet saying: “In his days righteousness shall rise, and abundance of peace.” And again, in our own day, he brings them in as having received each other, saying: “Mercy and truth have met; righteousness and peace have kissed.” For what so befits those who rule according to Christ, those who have taken up the office of bishop according to Christ, as peace and righteousness? And this, O lovers of Christ, is proclaimed far and wide by the prophet's voice. Hear God saying: “I will make your rulers peace and your overseers righteousness.”

Peace, then, has dawned. Let the heretical beasts flee. Peace has dawned. Let the savage packs of heretics run away. For just as wild beasts, having no boldness by day, take their liberty at night, so do those men, who cannot bear the brightness of peace. When a small cloud of pettiness passed over, it did not cut off peace but only cast it down [?]; and the beasts, thinking it was a moonless night, came out of their dens, bringing forth their own venom, and the word of David was fulfilled: “You made darkness, and it was night; in it all the beasts of the field will roam abroad; young lions roaring” to snatch a soul away from orthodoxy into false belief, from faith into unbelief, from truth into falsehood. But again—for he uses the same example—just as beasts that take their liberty at night run away as soon as they see the sunlight and return to their own lairs, so now too the saying of blessed David is fulfilled: “The sun of righteousness has risen, and they have gathered together and will lie down in their dens.”

Let us give thanks to Christ, who has settled the dust and sprinkled us with drops of peace and righteousness. For just as raindrops settle the dust, so drops of righteousness settle pettiness and dejection. That is why blessed Isaiah too prayed, saying: “Rejoice, O heaven above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness.” Let no one be troubled by what has gone before. “In a day of good things there is forgetfulness of evils.” Let no one be disturbed; let no one say: “Was it right for there to be pettiness among the priests of Christ?” Have we ceased to be human? Are we not often carried away by what we hear? You have an example that can console you. I am not insulting the saints—God forbid!—but I am showing human weaknesses from their example.

There was once a dispute between Paul and Barnabas, not with one side honouring righteousness and the other injustice, but with each side serving the aim of godliness. The cause of their pettiness was this. A certain Mark had travelled with them in preaching the Gospel from Palestine as far as Perga in Pamphylia. Then, as the apostles kept up their vigorous journey, with souls unbending in the face of struggles, battles and dangers, he took leave of the apostles' journey and went back to Palestine; he had not denied Christ, but, as has been said, he had excused himself from the long journey. Afterwards Paul and Barnabas came back, laden with the fruits of godliness and crowned with the labour of godliness, and they told the church in Jerusalem the good news of the conversion of all the Gentiles. While everyone was praising Paul and Barnabas for their achievements, Mark was stung; he was wounded in his soul. From then on he reasoned with himself this way, saying: “If I had shared in their labours, I would now be sharing in their praise.” For many people, though they often avoid virtues themselves because of the labour involved, choose to labour for the sake of the praise that comes from them. What then? Mark repented and resolved to travel with the apostles again when they set out. Barnabas at once received him on his repentance, but Paul disputed it and said: “We must not take along one who did not go with us to the work of the Lord.” So it was a quarrel not over injustice but between justice and friendship. Paul demanded what was just; Barnabas honoured what was kind. So, differing in judgement though they were agreed in godliness, they came to such sharp contention that they separated from each other. For so it is written: “They separated from each other.” They parted not in faith, nor in affection, but through human pettiness. Yet their parting came about by God's providence. Barnabas took Mark and set out on his journey, and Paul took Timothy and set out on his own journey. And Paul's strictness did Mark good. For when he saw himself cast off in this way because of his slackness, he was eager to cover his earlier sluggishness with zeal and with a second journey. So Mark went with Barnabas, toiling and running. Paul, for his part, instructed the churches not to receive Mark, not to hurt him but so that he would work more zealously. Then, when holy Paul saw Mark pressing ahead in zeal and making his amends to God by what he did afterwards, he began to commend him. And what does he say here? One phrase—and in it he gently reproves holy Barnabas for having treated Mark as a nephew and having been eager to pardon his fault as a nephew's. For what does he say? “Mark the nephew of Barnabas greets you, about whom you received instructions; if he comes, receive him.”

Now, then, let these ancient events console us in our present circumstances. If there was pettiness between Paul and Barnabas, what wonder if there is pettiness between us? But just as Mark, who stood in the middle then, both tried to turn back and was found worthy of kindness, so now let those who stand in the middle be received. Let them find God merciful. Christ will forgive everyone, and he will have mercy on me along with you. And let us ask our common father to set his seal on our word of peace, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
